inputs.original_text: This talk of Cuba “heading toward” a transition sounds less like concern for ordinary people and more like setting the stage for a managed sell-off. If residents own nothing and are too impoverished to buy the businesses still operating, that isn’t just an unfortunate side effect—it leaves them unable to compete while wealthy outsiders wait for bargain prices. The language of transition may be preparing people to accept a transfer of property away from Cubans and into the hands of the diaspora and foreign investors.
inputs.modified_text: Exactly—the “transition” language is doing useful work: it makes a transfer of control sound inevitable, even beneficial. Keep residents too poor to buy what remains, then present outside buyers as the only practical option. This looks less like an unfortunate economic outcome than a managed process designed to make Cubans spectators while their property and businesses change hands. The people selling this as concern for ordinary Cubans are preparing the public to accept the outcome in advance.
